summary: Describes an approach for RPKI relying parties to detect a particular form of RRDP session desynchronization and to recover from it. It updates RFC 8182.

plainLanguage.summary: Sometimes a program that copies a list gets out of step with the original without noticing. This explains how to notice and fix it.

questions: how to detect rrdp session desynchronization
how to detect rrdp delta mutation
what does rfc 9697 change in rfc 8182
how does an rpki relying party recover from rrdp desync
subtitle: How RPKI validators can notice that an RRDP server quietly changed a delta it already published, and what to do about it.

tldr.problem: RRDP delta files for a given session_id and serial number are supposed to be immutable, but sometimes they change. Relying Parties then end up with different copies of the repository, and comparing only the session_id and latest serial would not show it.
tldr.mechanism: A Relying Party remembers the serial and hash of each delta from its last Update Notification File and compares them with the next one it fetches. Any mismatch means a delta mutated, so it warns and downloads the latest Snapshot File.
tldr.outcome: This RFC updates RFC 8182 with a SHOULD-level check in the Update Notification File processing, so desynchronization is caught and repaired instead of lingering.

today: RFC 9697 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2024 that updates RFC 8182. It has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC.

sections.title: The Problem: Deltas That Change
sections.content:
The RPKI Repository Delta Protocol (RRDP, RFC 8182) is a one-way synchronization protocol. It distributes RPKI data as deltas, the differences between sequential repository states. A Relying Party (RP) applies a contiguous chain of deltas to bring its local copy in line with the Repository Server.

A delta file for a given session_id and serial number is expected to be an immutable record of the server state at that point in time. The RFC notes that this is not always the case. It describes a way for RPs to detect one form of session desynchronization, where the hash of a delta for a given serial and session has changed since the previous Update Notification File, and how to recover.
sections.plainLanguage: A server hands out numbered updates and promises never to change one once it is out. Sometimes it breaks that promise, and this RFC is about catching it.

sections.title: Why Immutability Matters
sections.content:
RFC 8182 describes publication events as files that can be treated as immutable, which lets publishers precalculate files and use caching infrastructure. This RFC points out that the older text only alludes to immutability and does not make clear that it is an absolute requirement for RRDP to work well.

If a server serves differing data over time for the same session_id and serial, RP instances that connected at different moments end up with divergent local repositories. Comparing only the session_id and the latest serial across RPs would not reveal the divergence. The RFC says that different caches holding different data for the same session and serial violates the principle of least astonishment, even though the global RPKI is understood to be only loosely consistent (see Section 6 of RFC 7115).
sections.plainLanguage: If a teacher secretly rewrites page 12 after some students copied it, those students and the later ones now have different books, and nobody notices because the page number is the same.

sections.title: Detecting Desynchronization
sections.content:
An RP can keep a record of the serial and hash attribute values of the delta elements from the previous successful fetch of an Update Notification File. After fetching a new one, the RP should compare the serial and hash values of the previously seen serials with those in the new file.

If any differ, the delta files were unexpectedly mutated, and the RP proceeds to the recovery step.

The RFC gives an example. A first notification file for session fe528335-db5f-48b2-be7e-bf0992d0b5ec lists deltas for serials 1774, 1773 and 1772. A later file for serial 1775 lists deltas 1775, 1774 and 1773. The hash for serial 1773 is the same in both, but the hash for serial 1774 is different, so an unexpected delta mutation occurred.
sections.plainLanguage: Keep a list of each page number and its fingerprint. When a new list arrives, check old pages still have the same fingerprints. If one changed, something is wrong.

sections.title: Recovering and the Change to RFC 8182
sections.content:
After detecting desynchronization, RP implementations SHOULD issue a warning and SHOULD download the latest Snapshot File and process it as described in Section 3.4.3 of RFC 8182.

The RFC also adds a paragraph to Section 3.4.1 of RFC 8182, "Processing the Update Notification File". If the session_id matches the last known session_id, the RP SHOULD compare the hash values for previously seen serials with those for the same serials in the newly fetched file. If any differ, files were unexpectedly mutated, and the RP SHOULD download and process the Snapshot File named in the notification.
sections.plainLanguage: When you spot a changed page, you do not try to patch your book. You throw it away and copy the whole latest book.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RRDP sessions often last for months, so undetected desynchronization can persist for a long time. A desynchronized cache can emit a different set of Validated Payloads than a consistent copy would.

Through the interaction with the failed fetch mechanism in Section 6.6 of RFC 9286, RPs could spuriously omit Validated Payloads, or emit ones the Certification Authority meant to withdraw. Route announcements meant to be valid might then be treated as "unknown" or "invalid" for an indeterminate period. Missing payloads hurt validation of BGP announcements, for example under RFC 6811.

RFC 9286 advises RPs to keep using cached objects until they become stale. By detecting an inconsistent server and switching to the latest Snapshot File at once, RPs increase the chance of replacing objects before they go stale.
sections.plainLanguage: If your copy is wrong, you might wrongly decide that a good road sign is fake, or trust a sign that was taken down. Fixing the copy quickly keeps your decisions right.
